compliance.notes: Comprehensive, well-constructed TMSS + Capital & Investment Strategy: capital expenditure/CFR (fully reconciled), authorised limit & operational boundary, a detailed asset-life MRP policy, a strong ratings-plus-CDS counterparty framework, borrowing strategy and a liability benchmark are all present - 23 of 24 core requirements score >=2. Weakest areas: no explicit formal adoption of the CIPFA TM Code's four clauses (GOV-01, the sole core gap), no separate HRA/General Fund liability benchmarks (LB-04) despite ~£203m HRA CFR, no exit-options review for the material service investments/company loans (COM-08, e.g. ~£210m Treveth), and no audit-qualification flag (RPT-05). The dominant substantive risk visible in the numbers is a very large short-term borrowing book (~£673m, ~43% of external debt) funding a fast-rising CFR (to ~£2.36bn by 2030/31).

news_drafts.headline: Cornwall forecasts £10.9m overspend after savings, down from £17m; collection fund gap of £10.1m–£21.6m for 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Cornwall Council is forecasting a day-to-day budget overspend of £10.857m for 2026/27, after measures identified so far cut the first-quarter projection from £17.008m. The figures are in the Council Performance Report for the first three months of the year, which went to the council's Cabinet on 23 September and is cited in a paper for an Individual Decision Day on 14 October.

That paper, on consulting over a revised Council Tax Reduction Scheme, also sets out a separate pressure on next year's budget. The council's refresh of its medium-term financial plan (its financial plan for the coming years) forecasts a gap of between £10.1m and £21.6m in 2027/28 on the collection fund, the account that records council tax and business rates income. The papers say the main driver is the retrospective reclassification of properties as self-catering accommodation for business rates. That requires backdated council tax refunds, which the business rates system does not fully offset.

The papers say the council is working with MPs to escalate the matter to Government. The 14 October decision concerns approval to consult on the proposed changes to the Council Tax Reduction Scheme.
news_drafts.paper_title: Individual Decision - Approval to consult on proposed revised Council Tax Reduction Scheme

news_drafts.headline: Cornwall Council has three LOBO loans worth £19m with lender call dates in July–September 2026
news_drafts.lead:
Cornwall Council has three LOBO loans, together worth £19m, whose lenders had the right to propose a new interest rate between July and September 2026. A LOBO loan is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. The figures come from the treasury report in the council's first-quarter performance report for 2026/27.

The three loans are part of a larger holding. The council has 10 LOBO loans totalling £168.2m, which is 10.3% of its total borrowing. The report says that when a lender calls a loan and proposes a new rate, the council can accept it or repay the loan at par, meaning at its face value and without penalty. The paper states the council has not recorded accepting a higher rate on any of its LOBOs.

The report says: "There are three LOBO's totalling £19m with call options dated within the next quarter of 2026/27." The papers do not say whether any of the three lenders proposed a new rate in that period, or what the council would do if one did.
news_drafts.paper_title: Council Performance Report 2026/27 (Q1) - Appendix 9 - 2026-27 Treasury Q1 Report

news_drafts.headline: Cornwall spends £10m a year on temporary housing as register trebles despite record delivery
news_drafts.lead: Cornwall Council is spending approximately £10 million a year on temporary and emergency accommodation for more than 800 people, even as it achieves record housing delivery. The council's social housing register has grown from around 9,000 households in March 2020 to approximately 25,000 today—an increase of 178 per cent in six and a half years. In 2025/26, the council delivered 824 affordable homes, the highest annual total since before the pandemic. Yet the register continues to grow. The council receives around 500 new applications each month but can house only approximately 120 households, leaving a structural gap between demand and supply that shows no sign of closing.
news_drafts.paper_title: A Fairer, Clearer Housing List for Cornwall - Report

findings.committee: Budget Development Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Budget Development OSC - 21 January 2026 - Draft Minutes
findings.headline: General Fund reserves declining at rate of change indicating higher risk; draft budget includes no provision to replenish reserves
findings.detail: The council's reserve levels as a percentage of net revenue expenditure fall within the mid-range of risk nationally, but the rate of change in reserves over recent years indicates a higher level of risk, a concern previously highlighted to the Committee. This is reinforced by the draft budget including no new transfer of funds to the General Fund reserve, indicating all available resources are directed to closing the budget gap and delivering services.
findings.matters: Declining reserves with no planned replenishment is a key sustainability signal lenders track closely; the trajectory of reserve depletion indicates financial resilience is weakening at a time when budget pressures are increasing.
findings.figures: Mid-range risk by reserve level nationally; higher risk indicated by rate of change over recent years
findings.quote: The Council was assessed as falling broadly within the mid -range of risk nationally, although with a higher level of risk was indicated by the rate of change in reserves over recent years, which had previously been highlighted to the Committee.

findings.committee: Budget Development Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Budget Development OSC - 21 January 2026 - Draft Minutes
findings.headline: Capital programme contingency increased by £7.2 million to £10 million total for 2026/27, reflecting programme volatility
findings.detail: The draft capital programme contingency is proposed to increase from £1.9m in 2025/26 to £10m in 2026/27. This £7.2m increase is justified by the scale of the capital programme (approximately 300 schemes per annum) and by the fact that part of the original £10m contingency in 2025/26 had already been called upon during the year to settle a contract.
findings.matters: The magnitude of contingency increase indicates capital programme volatility and delivery risk; lenders assess capital management capability through contingency sizing and call-down patterns.
findings.figures: £7.2 million increase; £10 million total for 2026/27; £1.9 million in 2025/26; approximately 300 schemes per annum
findings.quote: the question was asked as to the rationale of the proposed increase by £7.2 million in 2026/27 that would bring the contingency to a total of £10 million, given that the level for 2025/26 was £1.9 million.

findings.committee: Budget Development Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Budget Development OSC - 21 January 2026 - Draft Minutes
findings.headline: Council tax projected to provide over 60% of core spending power by 2028/29, above England average of approximately 55%
findings.detail: The council is heavily reliant on council tax income, with projections showing over 60% of core spending power derived from council tax by 2028/29. This is significantly above the England average of approximately 55%, indicating reduced flexibility in the council's funding structure and limited policy options for managing budget pressures without raising household bills.
findings.matters: Higher council tax dependency creates structural vulnerability; councils with similar dependency ratios face constrained choices in responding to funding pressure.
findings.quote: the Council remained heavily reliant on council tax income, with over 60% of core spending power derived from council tax by 2028/29, compared with an England average of approximately 55%.

findings.committee: Budget Development Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Budget Development OSC - 21 January 2026 - Draft Minutes
findings.headline: Government funding excluding council tax increases only 4.5% over three years, representing real-terms reduction
findings.detail: While headline spending power is projected to increase 27% to £198m, this is heavily dependent on council tax income. When council tax is excluded, Government funding increases by only £16m (4.5%) over the three-year settlement period, which represents a real-terms reduction given inflation and service pressure.
findings.matters: Shows that underlying government funding pressure is more severe than headline figures suggest; other councils and lenders track real-terms changes in core funding as a key indicator of sustainability.
findings.figures: £16 million (4.5%) core funding increase over three years; 27% headline spending power increase to £198 million
findings.quote: It was highlighted that, excluding council tax, Government funding increased by only £16 million (4.5%) over three years, representing a real -terms reduction.

findings.committee: Budget Development Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Budget Development OSC - 21 January 2026 - Draft Minutes
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast to reach approximately £250 million by 2029, with potential requirement for council contribution from 2028/29
findings.detail: The DSG deficit is growing significantly and by the end of the Medium-Term Financial Plan period (2029) is forecast to reach approximately £250 million. Officers are working with Cabinet to consider assumptions about potential council contribution from 2028/29, as early indications suggest the Government is unlikely to fully write off the deficit as originally hoped.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit represents a substantial contingent liability; lenders need to understand whether and when it may become a real call on the council's finances and how it affects long-term sustainability, particularly if it requires annual contributions from revenue.
findings.figures: £250 million by end of Medium-Term Financial Plan (2029)
findings.quote: the DSG deficit was forecast to increase to approximately £250 million by the end of the Medium -Term Financial Plan period in 2029.
